chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr from Sabbah al-Hazza' from Isma'il ibn 'Ammar who said:

I said to Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him), 'Inform me about a man in the state of Ihram (Muhrim) who had intercourse with his female slave who was also in the state of Ihram.' He said, 'Is he wealthy (Musr) or poor (Mu'sir)?' I said, 'Answer me for both.' He said, 'Did he command her to enter Ihram, or did he not command her, or did she enter Ihram on her own accord?' I said, 'Answer me for both.' He said, 'If he was wealthy, knew that it was not proper for him, and was the one who commanded her to enter Ihram, then upon him is a camel, and if he wishes, a cow, and if he wishes, a sheep. And if he did not command her to enter Ihram, then there is nothing upon him whether he was wealthy or poor. And if he commanded her and he was poor, then upon him is the blood of a sheep or fasting.'

key_terms.بَدَنَةٌ: A camel (specific type of sacrificial animal)
key_terms.دَمُ شَاةٍ: The blood of a sheep (referring to slaughtering a sheep as expiation)
key_terms.مُحِلٍّ: A man in the state of Ihram (ritual consecration for Hajj/Umrah)

ai.seo_question: What is the expiation for a man having intercourse with his female slave while both are in Ihram?
ai.summary: In this narration from Imam Musa al-Kazim (AS), the jurist distinguishes between the financial capacity (musir) and insolvency (mu'sir) of the master, linking the severity of the expiation—ranging from a camel to a sheep or fasting—to his knowledge of the prohibition and whether he initiated the slave's Ihram. This highlights the Shia legal principle that liability is modulated by both economic status and the specific causal role in the ritual violation, offering a nuanced application of Quranic injunctions on Hajj penalties.
